# US state privacy statutes: what a notice has to say

A working reference for [the notice review](../SKILL.md). It covers the four statutes that drive
most of our reviews. Confirm the current position before relying on any row: these laws are amended
often.

## The statutes

| State | Statute | In force since | Response deadline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| California | California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), as amended by the CPRA | January 1, 2020 | 45 days, one 45-day extension |
| Virginia | Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act (VCDPA) | January 1, 2023 | 45 days, one 45-day extension |
| Colorado | Colorado Consumer Data Protection Act (CCDPA) | July 1, 2023 | 45 days, one 45-day extension |
| Connecticut | Connecticut Data Privacy Act (CTDPA) | July 1, 2023 | 45 days, one 45-day extension |

These deadlines are commonly misread as calendar months. They are not: the clock is 45 days
from receipt of a verifiable request, and the single extension is another 45 days, granted only
where the request is complex and the consumer is told why.

## Universal opt-out mechanisms

The Colorado statute requires a controller to recognize a universal opt-out mechanism, an
opt-out signal the browser or the device sends on the consumer's behalf, from July 1, 2024. A
notice that offers only a web form and no signal recognition is out of date for Colorado consumers
even when the form works.

## Direction of consent

The GDPR and the US state statutes pull in opposite directions here, and mixing them up is the most
common drafting error we see in a notice written for both audiences.

Under the GDPR, a controller may send direct marketing email to an individual until that individual
objects, so a notice written for EU readers needs a clear objection route rather than a consent
gate. Colorado and Virginia run the other way: the consumer must opt in before any targeted
advertising, so a notice written for those states needs a consent banner and a record of the
consent that a regulator can inspect.

Write the notice for the stricter of the two audiences you actually have, and say in the notice
which regime each section is written under.

## Sensitive data

All four statutes treat a defined set of categories as sensitive: precise geolocation, biometric
identifiers processed to identify a person, health data, and data revealing racial or ethnic
origin, religious beliefs, or sexual orientation. A notice that lumps these in with the general
collection list does not disclose them, so item 1 of the checklist fails.
